newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovakia to trade foreign issues, brokers mixed.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia to trade foreign issues, brokers mixed.

text.p: Slovak stockbrokers on Tuesday welcomed a new securities law allowing trading foreign issues on the Slovak market, but warned the new shares may steal the limelight from local equities.
On Tuesday, the Slovak government approved an amendment to the securities' law opening the domestic market to foreign securities.
"These foreign issues will be traded on the Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE)," said Dusan Koledzaj, head of the Capital market division of the Finance Ministry.
The amendment is still subject to parliamentary approval.
"If parliament approves this law it will certainly increase the attractiveness of this market," Radovan Dzugas of Creditanstalt said.

Up to now, foreign issues could be traded only with the permission of the finance ministry. The new amendment, which brings the current securities law in line with OECD standards, overrides this requirement.
Slovakia is a candidate for OECD membership which is to be decided later this year.

The Slovak capital market has been constantly suffering from a significant lack of liquidity, with traders complaining over the reluctance of the domestic companies to enter the market with new share issues.
Brokers said the positive effect of the law would not lie only in the increase of liquidity of domestic issues but also in the improvement of the Slovak market's image.
"This is really good news even though it could bring some possible negative side effects," Dusan Sykora of ING Barings told Reuters.

"(But) we have to welcome any such liberalisation, because it will, if nothing else, give domestic investors an opportunity to enter some foreign markets," Sykora said. Koledzaj said the finance ministry had so far not received any request to trade foreign securities in Slovakia. But, he added, the ministry did not expect a massive inflow of foreign securities to Slovakia.
"I don't expect a massive inflow of foreign issues to Bratislava, but rather the flight of the few domestic investors to the Polish, Hungarian or Czech markets," Sykora warned.
"From this point of view this could even have a disastrous effect on the domestic market," he added.
